title: Azure Administrator (AZ-104)
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Microsoft. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: Locked out at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: A remote employee forgets their password on a Saturday night. The help desk is closed until Monday, and the employee can't work.
scenarios.prompt: What should the administrator enable so users can recover on their own?
choices: Self-service password reset (SSPR) with authentication methods registered
A Conditional Access policy blocking legacy auth
Password hash sync without SSPR
An access review for the user
scenarios.why: SSPR lets users reset their own passwords after verifying via registered authentication methods (Microsoft Authenticator, phone, etc.). It requires the methods be registered in advance and SSPR enabled for the users — the classic help-desk ticket reducer.
scenarios.hint: What feature lets a user prove who they are and reset their own password?

scenarios.title: The ever-changing team
scenarios.situation: The sales department has constant turnover. An admin manually adds each new hire to five security groups and always misses one.
scenarios.prompt: What eliminates the manual group maintenance?
choices: A dynamic security group with a membership rule like user.department -eq 'Sales'
A Microsoft 365 group with manual membership
An administrative unit per salesperson
A Conditional Access policy per user
scenarios.why: Dynamic groups evaluate membership rules against user attributes automatically — new hires with department=Sales join instantly, departures leave. This removes the human-error-prone manual process entirely.
scenarios.hint: What group type updates its own membership from user attributes?

scenarios.title: The external contractor
scenarios.situation: A contractor with a personal Gmail address needs access to one SharePoint site and one internal app for three months — no company laptop, no corporate account.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right identity approach?
choices: Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration — invite the Gmail identity as a guest with scoped access
Create a full member account with a company email
Share an existing employee's credentials
Open the SharePoint site to anonymous links permanently
scenarios.why: Entra B2B lets external users authenticate with their own identity (even a Gmail-backed account) as guests, with access scoped to specific resources and governed by Conditional Access and access reviews. No shared credentials, no over-provisioning.
scenarios.hint: Which feature is purpose-built for external users keeping their own identities?

scenarios.title: The phished password
scenarios.situation: An attacker phishes an employee's password but still can't sign in. The security team confirms the account had an extra verification step enforced.
scenarios.prompt: What stopped the attacker, and which method is strongest?
choices: Multifactor authentication; phishing-resistant methods like FIDO2 keys or certificate-based auth beat SMS codes
Password complexity requirements alone
A longer password expiration policy
Conditional Access without any MFA grant
scenarios.why: MFA requires a second factor beyond the password, so a stolen password alone is useless. Not all MFA is equal: FIDO2 security keys and Windows Hello for Business resist phishing, while SMS codes can be intercepted — a key exam distinction.
scenarios.hint: The password was compromised but sign-in still failed. What adds the second proof, and which kinds can't be phished?

scenarios.title: The risky sign-in
scenarios.situation: Sign-in logs show logins from an unusual country minutes after a legitimate login from headquarters. The admin wants risky sign-ins to require MFA automatically.
evidence: user: ana@contoso.com | location: Lagos, NG | risk: High | 14:02
user: ana@contoso.com | location: Boston, US | risk: None | 13:47
choices: A Conditional Access policy using the sign-in risk signal with a 'require MFA' grant
An RBAC role assignment on the user
A resource lock on the tenant
A password policy change
scenarios.why: Conditional Access evaluates signals (user/group, location, device, sign-in risk from Identity Protection) and enforces grants like require MFA or block. Risk-based policies are the standard response to impossible-travel and leaked-credential signals.
scenarios.hint: Which policy engine turns signals like 'risky sign-in' into required actions?

scenarios.title: License sprawl
scenarios.situation: IT assigns Microsoft 365 E5 licenses one by one in the portal. New hires wait days for Teams and mailbox provisioning.
choices: Group-based licensing — assign licenses to a group and membership drives provisioning
Buying more licenses
Assigning licenses via Conditional Access
Creating a separate tenant per department
scenarios.why: Group-based licensing assigns licenses to a group; anyone joining the group is licensed automatically (and deprovisioned on leaving). Combined with dynamic groups, onboarding becomes zero-touch.
scenarios.hint: What assignment target makes licensing follow group membership automatically?

scenarios.title: The over-privileged intern
scenarios.situation: An intern was made Contributor on the production subscription 'to get things started' and can now delete databases.
choices: Assign a narrower role (e.g., Reader, or a scoped custom role) at the resource-group scope instead of subscription Contributor
Remove all roles and use shared admin credentials
Keep Contributor but add a resource lock
Move the intern to a different tenant
scenarios.why: RBAC follows least privilege: grant the smallest role at the narrowest scope that still lets the person work. Contributor at subscription scope is far too broad for an intern; Reader or a scoped role at the resource-group level fits.
scenarios.hint: Which two dials — role and scope — do you turn down here?

scenarios.title: The backup operator
scenarios.situation: No built-in role matches the backup team: they need to trigger backups and restores but must not modify VMs or networking.
choices: A custom RBAC role with only the required Microsoft.RecoveryServices permissions
A new subscription for the backup team
A Conditional Access policy for backup operators
A management group per VM
scenarios.why: Custom roles define exact allowed actions (Actions/NotActions/DataActions) when built-in roles are too broad or too narrow. The backup-operator scenario is the textbook custom-role case.
scenarios.hint: Built-in roles don't fit. What RBAC construct lets you define exact permissions?

scenarios.title: The wrong region
scenarios.situation: Developers keep deploying storage accounts in regions outside the company's approved list, violating data-residency commitments.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces the allowed-regions rule automatically?
choices: An Azure Policy with a deny effect on the allowed-locations definition
An RBAC assignment removing Contributor
A resource lock on each storage account
A VNet service endpoint
scenarios.why: Azure Policy's built-in 'Allowed locations' definition with deny effect blocks non-compliant deployments at creation time and flags existing ones as non-compliant. RBAC controls who deploys; Policy controls what may be deployed.
scenarios.hint: You need to block the deployment itself, not the person. Which control evaluates the resource?

scenarios.title: Encrypt them all
scenarios.situation: A policy audit finds 200 existing storage accounts without secure transfer required. New ones are blocked, but the old ones remain.
scenarios.prompt: How does the admin fix the existing non-compliant resources at scale?
choices: A remediation task with a managed identity on a deployIfNotExists policy
Manually editing each storage account
Deleting and recreating the accounts
Opening a support ticket per account
scenarios.why: deployIfNotExists policies can auto-remediate: creating a remediation task runs the deployment template against non-compliant resources using the policy's managed identity. Deny only stops new deployments; remediation fixes the past.
scenarios.hint: Deny stops the future. What policy effect plus task fixes what's already there?

scenarios.title: The frozen network
scenarios.situation: The core hub VNet must never be modified or deleted, but monitoring tools still need to read its configuration.
choices: ReadOnly — blocks writes and deletes while allowing reads
CanNotDelete — blocks deletes but still allows modifications
No locks; use RBAC Reader instead
A policy with audit effect
scenarios.why: ReadOnly locks prevent any modification or deletion while permitting reads — exactly right for immutable shared infrastructure. CanNotDelete still allows configuration changes, which the scenario forbids.
scenarios.hint: Reads yes, changes no, deletes no. Which lock is the strictest?

scenarios.title: Missing cost centers
scenarios.situation: Finance requires a 'CostCenter' tag on every resource, but half the resources lack it.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces the tag going forward and identifies the gaps?
choices: A 'Require tag' policy (deny or modify) plus compliance reporting
A resource lock named CostCenter
An RBAC role called Tag Contributor
Renaming resources to include the cost center
scenarios.why: Azure Policy's tag requirements (built-in 'Require a tag and its value') can deny untagged deployments or append the tag via modify, and the compliance dashboard lists every non-compliant resource for cleanup.
scenarios.hint: Which control can both block untagged deployments and report existing gaps?

scenarios.title: The datacenter fire
scenarios.situation: A customer needs storage that survives the complete loss of one Azure datacenter within a region, but doesn't need cross-region copies.
choices: Zone-redundant storage (ZRS) — three copies across availability zones in the region
Locally-redundant storage (LRS) — three copies in one datacenter
Geo-redundant storage (GRS) — adds a second region
Premium page blobs
scenarios.why: ZRS synchronously replicates three copies across availability zones in the primary region — surviving a datacenter loss without paying for a second region. LRS keeps all copies in one facility; GRS/RA-GRS add the paired region.
scenarios.hint: Same region, multiple buildings. Which option spreads copies across zones?

scenarios.title: The cold archive
scenarios.situation: Seven years of compliance logs are almost never read but must be retained. They're currently on Hot tier and the bill is painful.
choices: Move them to Archive tier (offline) with a lifecycle management policy automating the transition
Move them to Cool tier and leave them
Delete them after one year
Enable soft delete instead
scenarios.why: Archive is the cheapest tier for rarely-accessed data (rehydration takes hours). Lifecycle management policies automate tier transitions by age — e.g., Hot→Cool after 30 days, →Archive after 180 — so nobody does it manually.
scenarios.hint: Almost never read, must be kept, cheapest wins. Which tier, and how do you automate the move?

scenarios.title: The partner upload
scenarios.situation: A partner needs to upload files to one blob container for the next 48 hours only — no portal access, no account keys.
choices: A service SAS token scoped to the container with write permission and a 48-hour expiry
The storage account key emailed to the partner
Making the container publicly readable
A full Contributor RBAC role
scenarios.why: Shared access signatures grant constrained, time-limited access (permissions, IP, expiry) without exposing account keys. A service SAS on the container with write-only for 48 hours is the least-privilege answer; keys and RBAC are far too broad.
scenarios.hint: Time-boxed, scoped, no keys shared. Which token does that?

scenarios.title: Ten terabytes to move
scenarios.situation: An admin must migrate 10 TB from on-premises file shares to Azure Blob storage with resume capability and parallel transfers.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool is built for this?
choices: AzCopy — multi-threaded copy with resume, sync, and benchmark support
Azure Storage Explorer for 10 TB bulk loads
Manual portal uploads
Az PowerShell New-AzStorageBlob one file at a time
scenarios.why: AzCopy is the purpose-built high-performance copy tool (azcopy copy/sync), multi-threaded with automatic resume on failure. Storage Explorer is fine for small interactive work but not 10 TB bulk migration.
scenarios.hint: Bulk, resumable, parallel — which CLI tool is designed for exactly this?

scenarios.title: The open storage account
scenarios.situation: A storage account allows access from any network. The security team wants only the corporate VNet and the office IP range to reach it.
scenarios.prompt: What restricts network access to the storage account?
choices: Storage firewall: deny default network access, allow the VNet and specific IPs
A resource lock
Enabling blob versioning
Switching to Hot tier
scenarios.why: The storage account firewall (Firewalls and virtual networks) defaults to deny and whitelists VNets (via service endpoints/private endpoints) and IP ranges. This is network-layer control independent of SAS keys or RBAC.
scenarios.hint: Which setting turns 'the whole internet' into 'only these networks'?

scenarios.title: The overwritten blob
scenarios.situation: A script overwrites a critical blob with bad data. The team needs yesterday's version back.
scenarios.prompt: Which features would have saved them?
choices: Blob versioning or soft delete — recover prior versions/deleted blobs within retention
Geo-redundancy — replicates the bad overwrite too
A resource lock — blocks all writes including legitimate ones
Cool tier — cheaper but doesn't version
scenarios.why: Soft delete retains deleted blobs for the retention period; versioning keeps every overwritten version automatically. Geo-replication copies the corruption along — redundancy is not backup or versioning.
scenarios.hint: Redundancy copies the mistake. What keeps the old versions?

scenarios.title: The wrong VM size
scenarios.situation: A memory-hungry analytics app was deployed on a compute-optimized F-series VM and keeps running out of RAM while CPU sits idle.
choices: F-series is compute-optimized; a memory-optimized E-series fits this workload
All VM series are identical; the app needs more disks
The VM needs an availability set, not a resize
F-series is storage-optimized
scenarios.why: VM series encode their optimization: F = compute, E/D = memory (E has higher memory-to-CPU), L = storage, N = GPU. A memory-bound app on F-series wastes CPU while starving for RAM — resize to E-series.
scenarios.hint: Which series letter means 'built for memory-heavy workloads'?

scenarios.title: The single VM outage
scenarios.situation: A critical app runs on one VM with a 99.9% SLA. Leadership wants 99.99% for the VM tier.
scenarios.prompt: What change earns the higher SLA?
choices: Deploy two or more VMs across availability zones behind a load balancer
Add a bigger OS disk
Enable boot diagnostics
Move the VM to a different region
scenarios.why: Azure's SLA for VMs reaches 99.99% with two or more instances across availability zones. A single VM caps at 99.9% regardless of size — redundancy, not bigger hardware, raises the SLA.
scenarios.hint: What does the SLA require beyond one VM?

scenarios.title: The spiky web tier
scenarios.situation: A web tier needs between 3 and 20 identical VMs depending on traffic, with new instances configured identically and automatically.
choices: Virtual Machine Scale Sets with autoscale rules
An availability set
Manual VM creation per spike
A single large VM
scenarios.why: VMSS manages identical VMs as a set with autoscale based on metrics (CPU, queue length), plus rolling upgrades. Availability sets provide fault/update domain spread but no scaling or identical-image management.
scenarios.hint: Identical VMs that grow and shrink automatically — which construct?

scenarios.title: The exposed RDP port
scenarios.situation: Admins RDP to VMs over the public internet with NSG rules open to the world. Security flags this immediately.
choices: Azure Bastion — browser/portal-based RDP/SSH through the Azure fabric with no public IPs on VMs
A wider NSG rule
A VPN gateway for every admin laptop
Disabling RDP entirely
scenarios.why: Bastion provides RDP/SSH via the Azure portal over TLS without public IPs or exposed ports on the VMs. It's the managed alternative to jump boxes with internet-facing management ports.
scenarios.hint: How do admins reach VMs with zero public management ports?

scenarios.title: The busy database disk
scenarios.situation: A database VM's data disk hits throughput limits during peak load. The OS disk is fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right storage move?
choices: Move the data to Premium SSD (or Ultra Disk) sized for the required IOPS/throughput — disk performance scales with size and type
Add more vCPUs to the VM
Enable page file on the temp disk
Switch the OS disk to Standard HDD
scenarios.why: Managed disk performance (IOPS and MB/s) is determined by disk type and size: Premium SSD tiers scale with provisioned size, Ultra Disk allows independent tuning. Compute changes don't fix a disk bottleneck.
scenarios.hint: The bottleneck is disk throughput. What determines a managed disk's IOPS?

scenarios.title: The fleet configuration
scenarios.situation: Two hundred VMs need the same monitoring agent and a custom script run at deployment, consistently.
choices: VM extensions (Custom Script Extension, Azure Monitor agent) deployed via policy or template
RDP into each VM
A runbook that emails instructions
Bastion sessions per VM
scenarios.why: VM extensions install and configure software post-deployment (Custom Script Extension runs scripts; Azure Monitor Agent ships telemetry), deployable at scale through ARM/Bicep or Policy. Manual per-VM work doesn't scale.
scenarios.hint: What mechanism runs scripts and installs agents across a VM fleet automatically?

scenarios.title: The blocked web traffic
scenarios.situation: A web server VM answers on localhost but not from the internet. The NSG has an allow rule for port 80 with priority 200, and a deny-all rule with priority 100.
choices: Lower priority numbers win — the deny at 100 is evaluated before the allow at 200
NSGs don't apply to port 80
Priority numbers are ignored for inbound rules
The VM needs a public IP on localhost
scenarios.why: NSG rules are processed in priority order, lowest number first; the first match decides. A deny-all at priority 100 shadows the allow at 200 — the classic NSG misconfiguration. (Also check: is there an allow for the health probe/load balancer?)
scenarios.hint: Rules are evaluated top-down by priority number. Which rule matches first?

scenarios.title: Two VNets, no transit
scenarios.situation: VNet-A peers with VNet-B, and VNet-B peers with VNet-C. A VM in VNet-A can't reach VNet-C.
choices: VNet peering is non-transitive — A↔B and B↔C peerings don't create an A↔C path
Peering requires identical address spaces
VMs can't cross peerings without VPN gateways
Peering only works within one resource group
scenarios.why: Peering is strictly point-to-point and non-transitive. A-to-C needs its own peering (or a hub VNet with routing/NVA). Overlapping address spaces would actually prevent peering from being created at all.
scenarios.hint: If A peers B and B peers C, does A reach C automatically?

scenarios.title: The datacenter link
scenarios.situation: A company needs a private, high-throughput, low-latency connection from its datacenter to Azure for daily 5 TB database replication.
choices: ExpressRoute — private dedicated connectivity with consistent throughput
Site-to-site VPN over the public internet
Point-to-site VPN per user
VNet peering to the on-premises network
scenarios.why: ExpressRoute provides private, dedicated bandwidth (up to 100 Gbps) with SLA-backed latency — right for bulk replication. S2S VPN rides the public internet with variable throughput; peering only connects Azure VNets.
scenarios.hint: Bulk replication needs consistent private throughput. Which option isn't over the public internet?

scenarios.title: The PaaS data leak
scenarios.situation: An Azure SQL database has a public endpoint. The architect wants all traffic to stay on the private VNet with no public exposure.
scenarios.prompt: What provides private connectivity to the PaaS service?
evidence: no public IP on SQL logical server; app VMs in VNet 'prod-vnet' only
choices: A private endpoint — a NIC in the VNet with a private IP mapping to the SQL server via Private Link
A service endpoint — which keeps traffic on the backbone but the SQL endpoint stays public
An NSG on the database
A VPN gateway
scenarios.why: Private endpoints bring the PaaS service into your VNet with a private IP (resolving via private DNS zone), eliminating public endpoint exposure. Service endpoints extend VNet identity to the service but the public endpoint remains.
scenarios.hint: Which option gives the SQL server an address inside your VNet?

scenarios.title: The unresolvable name
scenarios.situation: VMs in a VNet can't resolve each other's hostnames after the admin pointed the VNet at an on-premises DNS server that knows nothing about Azure names.
choices: Use Azure-provided DNS (168.63.129.16) or add conditional forwarders for the Azure zones
Add more NSG rules
Enable IP forwarding on the VMs
Create a private endpoint for DNS
scenarios.why: Azure-provided DNS automatically resolves VM hostnames within the VNet. Pointing the VNet at an external DNS that lacks Azure records breaks internal resolution — fix by reverting to Azure DNS or configuring conditional forwarding for internal zones.
scenarios.hint: Who was resolving names before, and what changed?

scenarios.title: The /29 mistake
scenarios.situation: An admin creates a /29 subnet for an application tier, then finds only 3 usable IPs after Azure reserves addresses.
choices: Azure reserves 5 IPs per subnet (network, gateway, DNS x2, broadcast) — a /29 (8 addresses) leaves 3 usable
Subnets require a minimum /24
The subnet needs a NAT gateway first
Usable IPs equal total IPs in Azure
scenarios.why: Every Azure subnet loses 5 addresses to platform reservations (.0 network, .1 gateway, .2/.3 DNS, .255 broadcast). A /29 yields 8−5=3 usable — far too small for most tiers; size subnets for growth.
scenarios.hint: How many addresses does Azure reserve in every subnet?

scenarios.title: The CPU spike
scenarios.situation: An admin wants a near-real-time chart of VM CPU over the last hour, and separately wants to search six months of sign-in records for anomalies.
scenarios.prompt: Which data types fit each need?
choices: Metrics for the CPU chart (numeric time-series); logs for the sign-in search (queryable records)
Logs for both
Metrics for both
Resource Health for both
scenarios.why: Metrics are lightweight numeric time-series (great for charts and metric alerts); logs are rich records stored in Log Analytics workspaces and queried with KQL (great for forensic search). Pick the data type by the question you're asking.
scenarios.hint: Charting a number over time versus searching rich records — which data type is each?

scenarios.title: The failed sign-ins
scenarios.situation: The SOC wants the top 10 users with failed sign-ins in the last 7 days from the SigninLogs table.
choices: SigninLogs | where ResultType != 0 | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | summarize failures=count() by UserPrincipalName | top 10 by failures desc
SELECT TOP 10 * FROM SigninLogs WHERE failures
SigninLogs | take 10
Get-AzSigninLog -Top 10
scenarios.why: KQL pipelines: filter with where, aggregate with summarize ... by, rank with top. ResultType != 0 means failure in sign-in logs. SQL syntax doesn't work in Log Analytics.
scenarios.hint: Filter, group-count by user, take the top 10 — which pipeline does that?

scenarios.title: The disk-full warning
scenarios.situation: The team wants an email when any VM's OS disk exceeds 85% full, evaluated every 15 minutes.
choices: A metric alert rule on the Logical Disk % Free Space metric with an action group for email
A log alert running every 15 minutes on boot diagnostics
Azure Service Health alert
A policy assignment
scenarios.why: Metric alert rules evaluate platform/guest metrics on a frequency and fire action groups (email, SMS, webhooks, Logic Apps). Disk space is a guest metric (via Azure Monitor Agent); the action group delivers the notification.
scenarios.hint: Which alert type watches a numeric metric on a schedule and notifies a group?

scenarios.title: The silent packet drop
scenarios.situation: Traffic between two VMs in peered VNets is failing. NSGs look correct and the admin suspects routing.
scenarios.prompt: Which Network Watcher tool diagnoses the path?
choices: IP flow verify and next hop — test whether a packet is allowed and where it routes
Connection Monitor — for long-term latency stats only
Packet capture — only on the gateway
NSG flow logs — show allowed traffic only
scenarios.why: Network Watcher's IP flow verify simulates a packet against NSG rules, and 'next hop' reveals the effective route (system, UDR, or peering). Together they pinpoint whether security rules or routing drops the traffic.
scenarios.hint: You need to ask 'would this packet be allowed, and where would it go?' — which tool answers?

scenarios.title: Is it us or Azure?
scenarios.situation: Multiple VMs in East US report connectivity issues simultaneously. The admin's own configs haven't changed.
scenarios.prompt: Where do they check for a platform incident first?
choices: Azure Service Health — official status of Azure services by region
Resource Health — per-resource health, better for single-resource issues
Azure Monitor metrics — shows their own telemetry
The activity log — shows their own operations
scenarios.why: Service Health reports Azure platform incidents and planned maintenance per region — the first stop when many resources fail together with no config change. Resource Health drills into individual resources afterward.
scenarios.hint: Many resources, one region, no config change — platform or customer? Where is the platform status?

scenarios.title: The missing audit trail
scenarios.situation: After a security incident, the team discovers NSG flow logs and firewall logs were never enabled — there's no network audit trail.
scenarios.prompt: What should they configure going forward?
choices: Diagnostic settings routing NSG flow logs and Azure Firewall logs to a Log Analytics workspace
Enabling boot diagnostics on VMs
A longer metrics retention period
Resource locks on the NSGs
scenarios.why: Diagnostic settings stream platform logs (NSG flow logs via Traffic Analytics, firewall logs, etc.) to Log Analytics/Storage/Event Hubs for audit and investigation. Logging must be enabled before the incident — you can't query what was never collected.
scenarios.hint: Which setting decides where a resource's logs are sent?

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you troubleshot a production outage involving Azure infrastructure.
Describe a time you implemented least-privilege access and someone pushed back.
points: The access requested vs. what was needed

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you automated a repetitive Azure administration task.
Describe a migration or deployment that didn't go as planned.
points: What went wrong and the impact
What you changed in the process

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to explain a cloud bill or cost spike to leadership.
Describe a time you balanced security requirements with developer velocity.
pitfalls: Security theater with no real control

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you documented a system or runbook that others now rely on.
points: What was undocumented and the risk

behavioral.prompt: Why are you pursuing the Azure Administrator certification, and what administrator responsibilities are you targeting?
points: The admin scope you want to own
